body:
From medieval poetry to modern literature

Gujarati literature developed through religious traditions, devotional poetry, narrative compositions, social reform, nationalism and modern literary movements. Its history is broadly divided into the Medieval period (Madhyakalin Yug) and the Modern period (Arvachin Yug).

Early Gujarati literature developed from linguistic traditions associated with Prakrit and Apabhramsha. Jain scholars made important contributions to its preservation and development. Acharya Hemachandra's grammatical work, Siddha-Hema-Shabdanushasana, contains examples of Apabhramsha verse that are important for understanding the historical development of Gujarati.

The emergence of Narsinh Mehta in the 15th century marks an important stage in Gujarati devotional literature. Medieval authors subsequently developed several distinctive literary forms, including the pada, akhyana, chhappa, padyavarta and garbi. Around the middle of the 19th century, Narmad and Dalpatram helped establish modern Gujarati literature through social reform, new literary subjects and the expansion of prose writing.

Major literary periods

Literary periodApproximate periodPrincipal characteristics
Medieval periodBefore 1850Devotion, spiritual knowledge and narrative poetry
Sudharak Yug or Narmad Yug1850–1885Social reform and modern literary awakening
Pandit Yug or Sakshar Yug1885–1915Scholarship, philosophy and cultural reflection
Gandhi Yug1915–1940sNationalism, simplicity and social responsibility
Anu-Gandhi Yug1940s–1950sAesthetic exploration and individual experience
Adhunik YugMid-1950s onwardModernist experimentation and individual consciousness
Anu-Adhunik YugApproximately mid-1980s onwardDiverse identities, social experiences and literary approaches

These divisions identify dominant literary tendencies rather than fixed historical boundaries. An author may continue writing across several periods. Literary historians also differ slightly in their dating of particular eras.

Literary movements and pen names

Pragativad, or progressive literature, developed prominently during the Gandhian period and emphasized social and economic inequality. Dalit literature and feminist literature developed around questions of caste discrimination, gender inequality, dignity and identity. These are literary movements and approaches that can overlap with chronological periods.

A takhallus or upanam is a literary pen name used by an author. For example, Kalapi was the literary name of Sursinhji Takhtasinhji Gohil, while Dhumketu was the pen name of Gaurishankar Govardhanram Joshi.

Prelims focus

  • Narsinh Mehta is associated with medieval devotional literature.
  • Sudharak Yug is also called Narmad Yug.
  • Pandit Yug is also called Sakshar Yug or Govardhan Yug.
  • Suresh Joshi is a pioneering figure of Adhunik Gujarati literature.
  • Trap: Pragativad, Dalit literature and feminist literature are not necessarily separate, mutually exclusive chronological eras.

[References: IGNOU, Poetry, Unit 6, Section 6.2, printed p. 122; INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala, Indian Literary Criticism and Theory, Chapter 30, History of Gujarati Literature; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, English medium, Chapter 4, Literary Heritage of India, pp. 32–33. Online textbook copies were used because the scanned chapter pages of GPSC Books Volume 09 were inaccessible. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Major Eras and Development of Gujarati Literature

body:
Narsinh Mehta

Narsinh Mehta, also called Narasinh Mehta or Narsi Mehta, was a prominent 15th-century Gujarati saint-poet. Traditionally associated with Talaja and Junagadh in Saurashtra, he occupies a foundational position in Gujarati devotional poetry and is popularly known as the Adikavi of Gujarati literature.

The title Adikavi recognizes his foundational literary importance. It does not mean that Gujarati literature did not exist before him. Jain literary compositions and other early Gujarati works preceded his poetry.

Religious outlook and literary contribution

Narsinh's poetry belongs predominantly to the Sagun Bhakti tradition, in which the divine is worshipped through a personal form. His devotion centred on Krishna, but his poetry also emphasized compassion, humility and recognition of the suffering of others.

His compositions include padas, devotional songs, prabhatiyas and poems concerning Krishna's life and divine love. A pada is a lyrical verse composition, while a prabhatiya is a morning devotional song.

  • Vaishnav Jan To: A celebrated devotional composition emphasizing compassion, moral conduct and sensitivity towards others.
  • Jhulana compositions: Devotional lyrics associated with Narsinh's poetic tradition.
  • Sudama Charitra: The narrative of Krishna and Sudama appears in the poetic tradition associated with Narsinh.

Vaishnav Jan To was particularly admired by Mahatma Gandhi. Its emphasis on empathy connects medieval devotional ethics with Gandhian ideas of service and moral responsibility.

Bhalan

Bhalan was a medieval Gujarati poet associated with Patan. He occupies an important place in the development of the akhyana and is commonly described as the father of the Gujarati akhyana.

An akhyana is an extended narrative poem that recounts a story, frequently drawn from the epics, Puranas or religious traditions. Unlike a short devotional lyric, it develops characters and successive events within a sustained narrative.

Bhalan made stories from Sanskrit literature accessible to Gujarati-speaking audiences. His use of the expression Gurjar Bhakha is an important association in the history of the Gujarati language.

Important works of Bhalan

WorkSubject or source
KadambariGujarati verse adaptation of Banabhatta's Sanskrit prose narrative
DhruvakhyanStory of Dhruva's devotion
Mrugi AkhyanStory derived from the Shaiva narrative tradition
NalakhyanNala and Damayanti from the Mahabharata
Jalandhar AkhyanPuranic narrative

Bhalan helped establish the akhyana as a significant Gujarati literary form. Premanand, a later poet of the 17th century, brought this narrative tradition to a high level of development.

Prelims focus

  • Narsinh Mehta: Adikavi, Krishna devotion and prabhatiyas.
  • Vaishnav Jan To: Narsinh Mehta.
  • Bhalan: Early development of Gujarati akhyana.
  • Bhalan: Patan and Gurjar Bhakha.
  • Kadambari: Bhalan adapted Banabhatta's Sanskrit work into Gujarati verse.
  • Trap: Bhalan was the early developer of the akhyana; Premanand was its later master.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 7, English medium, 2021–22 edition, Chapters 7–8, Bhakti Age: Religious Sects and Saints and Formation of Regional Culture; NCERT, Our Pasts II, Class 7, Devotional Paths to the Divine, pp. 104–121; Gujarati Vishwakosh, entries Bhalan and Gujarati Kavita; IGNOU, Poetry, Unit 6, Section 6.2, p. 122. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Devotional lyric and the development of narrative poetry.

title: Narsinh Mehta and Bhalan: Devotional Poetry and Akhyana

body:
Akho and the Jnanmargi tradition

Akho, also known as Akha Bhagat, was a 17th-century Gujarati saint-poet associated with Jetalpur and Ahmedabad. He came from a goldsmith community and became an important representative of the Jnanmargi, or knowledge-oriented, tradition of Gujarati literature.

Akho emphasized spiritual understanding and self-realization rather than dependence on outward rituals. His writings frequently criticize religious hypocrisy, meaningless ceremonies and the pretence of spiritual knowledge.

His philosophical outlook was influenced by Advaita Vedanta, which emphasizes the ultimate non-duality of reality. His poetry is associated with the knowledge-oriented and Nirgun traditions, although his literary outlook cannot be reduced simply to a rejection of devotion.

Principal compositions

  • Akha na Chhappa: Short, generally 6-line verse compositions containing philosophical observations, moral lessons and satire.
  • Akhe Gita: A philosophical composition dated to 1649, dealing with spiritual knowledge and realization.
  • Guru-Shishya Samvad: A composition presented through a dialogue between a teacher and disciple.
  • Anubhav Bindu: A philosophical work associated with spiritual experience and understanding.

Narsinh Mehta is especially associated with Krishna-centred devotional lyrics. Akho is especially associated with spiritual knowledge, philosophical instruction and satirical chhappas.

Premanand Bhatt and the mature akhyana

Premanand Bhatt was a major Gujarati narrative poet of the late 17th century associated with Vadodara. He developed the akhyana tradition through detailed storytelling, recognizable human emotions and the adaptation of traditional stories to Gujarati social life.

Although many of his narratives originated in Sanskrit epics and religious literature, they were not merely literal translations. He presented familiar stories through Gujarati language, customs and relationships, making them accessible to ordinary audiences.

Major works and their sources

WorkUnderlying narrative
Sudama CharitraKrishna and Sudama from the Bhagavata tradition
NalakhyanNala and Damayanti from the Mahabharata
MameruAn episode from the life of Narsinh Mehta
HundiAn episode associated with Narsinh Mehta's devotion
OkhaharanOkha or Usha and Aniruddha from the Krishna narrative tradition
RanayajnaEvents associated with the Ramayana
Dasham SkandhaThe tenth book of the Bhagavata Purana

Mameru presents the traditional occasion of gifts being given by a woman's maternal family. By connecting this custom with an episode involving Narsinh Mehta, Premanand brings together devotion and Gujarati family life.

Multiple versions of the same narrative

The existence of different Gujarati works with similar titles is an important feature of medieval literature. For example, Bhalan and Nakar composed versions of Nalakhyan before Premanand. Premanand's celebrated version is therefore not the only Gujarati rendering of the story of Nala and Damayanti.

Prelims focus

  • Akho: Jnanmargi poetry, chhappa and Akhe Gita.
  • Chhappa: Generally a 6-line verse composition.
  • Akhe Gita: 1649.
  • Premanand: Vadodara and the mature akhyana tradition.
  • Mameru and Hundi: Narratives involving Narsinh Mehta.
  • Trap: Both Bhalan and Premanand composed versions of Nalakhyan.

[References: Gujarati Vishwakosh, entries Akho, Akha na Chhappa, Premanand, Bhalan and Gujarati Kavita; IGNOU, Poetry, Unit 6, Section 6.2, p. 122. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The Mahabharata's Nala and Damayanti narrative led to earlier Gujarati versions by Bhalan and Nakar and a later celebrated version by Premanand.
pictures.caption: Different Gujarati versions of the Nala and Damayanti narrative.

title: Akho and Premanand: Spiritual Knowledge and Narrative Poetry

body:
Shamal Bhatt and the padyavarta

Shamal Bhatt, also written as Samal Bhatt or Shamal, was an important 18th-century Gujarati narrative poet associated with Ahmedabad. His principal contribution was to the padyavarta, a story narrated in verse.

Medieval akhyanas frequently drew upon religious and epic stories, while Shamal's padyavartas often emphasized adventure, imagination, practical intelligence, moral instruction and entertaining incidents. Although these literary forms can overlap, Shamal is particularly remembered for verse tales rather than philosophical chhappas or devotional garbis.

Principal works

WorkPrincipal association
Sinhasan Batrisi32 stories associated with King Vikramaditya and his throne
Vetala Pachisi25 tales associated with Vikramaditya and the Vetala narrative tradition
Suda BahoteriA collection associated with 72 tales
Chandrachandravatini VartaExtended verse narrative

Shamal's treatment of the Vetala stories is associated with his larger Sinhasan Batrisi narrative tradition. These compositions draw upon older Indian storytelling traditions, so Shamal should be understood as a major Gujarati adapter and narrator rather than the original inventor of every underlying story.

Dayaram and Krishna devotion

Dayaram (1777–1853) was one of the last major representatives of medieval Gujarati devotional poetry. He was born at Chanod, also called Chandod, and spent much of his life at Dabhoi in present-day Vadodara district.

Dayaram belonged to the Vaishnava Pushtimarg tradition associated with Vallabhacharya. Pushtimarg emphasizes devotion to Krishna and divine grace. Dayaram's lyrical compositions express devotion through the love of Radha and Krishna, longing for union with the divine and the emotions of Krishna's devotees.

Literary contribution

  • Garbi: Dayaram is especially celebrated for lyrical compositions expressing Krishna devotion and divine love.
  • Pada: His devotional lyrics also belong to the broader medieval tradition of padas.
  • Rasikvallabh: A philosophical and religious work explaining aspects of Pushtimarg devotion.
  • Bhakti Poshan: A composition associated with devotional teaching.

The terms garbo and garbi have related historical meanings. Garbo is often associated with goddess worship, while garbi is particularly associated with lyrical expressions of Krishna devotion in the work of poets such as Dayaram. This is a useful literary distinction, not an absolute rule governing every composition.

Medieval authors and their distinctive forms

The major medieval authors can be distinguished through their characteristic literary forms. Narsinh Mehta is remembered for padas and prabhatiyas; Bhalan and Premanand for akhyanas; Akho for chhappas and philosophical compositions; Shamal for padyavartas; and Dayaram for garbis.

Prelims focus

  • Shamal Bhatt: Padyavarta and Sinhasan Batrisi.
  • Vetala Pachisi and Suda Bahoteri: Shamal's narrative tradition.
  • Dayaram: 1777–1853, Chanod and Dabhoi.
  • Dayaram: Pushtimarg and Krishna-centred garbis.
  • Rasikvallabh: Dayaram.
  • Trap: Shamal's verse tales and Dayaram's devotional garbis represent different literary forms.

[References: Gujarati Vishwakosh, entries Shamal Bhatt, Sinhasan Batrisi, Padyavarta, Dayaram, Garbo-Garbi and Gujarati Kavita. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
